pillars.name: Operational Excellence
pillars.summary: Build software correctly and keep delivering a great customer experience. Automate safely, make small reversible changes, observe everything and learn from failure.

pillars.name: Security
pillars.summary: Protect data, systems and assets with strong identity and least privilege, traceability, encryption in transit and at rest, and defence in depth.

pillars.name: Reliability
pillars.summary: A reliable workload does its intended job correctly and consistently. It recovers from failure automatically, scales horizontally and has no single point of failure.

pillars.name: Performance Efficiency
pillars.summary: Use computing resources efficiently to meet requirements, even as demand changes. Pick the right resource types, go global in minutes, and prefer managed and serverless services.

pillars.name: Cost Optimization
pillars.summary: Deliver business value at the lowest price point. Pay only for what you use, right-size, measure spend and stop paying for idle resources.

pillars.name: Sustainability
pillars.summary: Minimise the environmental impact of running cloud workloads. Keep utilisation high, use managed services, and store and move less data.

puzzles.title: Thumbnail Factory
puzzles.story: The city photo club uploads hundreds of pictures a day and wants a small thumbnail of each one created automatically. Traffic is spiky: quiet all week, flooded after events.
requirements: Store original photos durably
Create a thumbnail automatically whenever a photo is uploaded
Pay nothing for compute when nobody is uploading
puzzles.why: An S3 event notification invokes a Lambda function on each upload. The function resizes the image and writes the thumbnail to a separate bucket or prefix. Never write back to the source prefix, or each thumbnail triggers the function again in a recursive loop. Lambda scales with uploads and costs nothing when idle, unlike an always-on EC2 server.
puzzles.simpleWhy: Each upload wakes Lambda to make a small copy, saved somewhere else so it doesn't loop forever. No uploads, no bill.

operational.tip: Alarm on Lambda errors and duration so you notice failed thumbnails before users do.

security.tip: Give the function a role that can only read the source prefix and write the thumbnail prefix.

reliability.tip: Buffer events through SQS with a dead-letter queue so bursts and bad images are retried or isolated.

performance.tip: Tune Lambda memory: more memory also means more CPU, often making image resizing faster.

cost.tip: Lambda costs nothing between uploads; S3 lifecycle rules move old originals to cheaper storage classes.

sustainability.tip: Event-driven compute runs only when there is work, so no servers sit idle burning energy.

rejects.efs: EFS is a shared file system you mount. S3 stores photos for less and sends upload events.

puzzles.title: The City Brochure Site
puzzles.story: The tourist office needs a fast website at www.awscity.example for visitors worldwide. It is just web pages, style sheets and images, with no server code.
requirements: Host static files cheaply and durably
Serve visitors from locations near them over HTTPS
Use the city's own domain name
Keep the storage bucket private
puzzles.why: Route 53 resolves the domain to a CloudFront distribution with an alias record. CloudFront caches content at edge locations and fetches it from a private S3 bucket using Origin Access Control. No servers are needed, S3 Block Public Access stays on, and caching makes the site fast and cheap.
puzzles.simpleWhy: Route 53 points the name at CloudFront, whose post offices keep copies of the site from a private S3 bucket. No servers needed.

operational.tip: Deploy site files from a pipeline and watch CloudFront error-rate metrics.

security.tip: Use Origin Access Control so only CloudFront can read the bucket, and add WAF rules at the edge.

reliability.tip: S3 is designed for 11 nines (99.999999999%) durability, and Route 53 is a highly available DNS service.

performance.tip: Edge caching serves users from nearby locations. Put a version in asset file names so you can cache them with long TTLs.

cost.tip: There are no servers to pay for. Cache hits cut origin requests, and data transfer from S3 to CloudFront is free.

sustainability.tip: Caching near users cuts repeated long-distance data transfer and origin work.

edges.caption: The browser connects to the nearest CloudFront edge location over HTTPS.

edges.caption: On a miss, CloudFront fetches the file. OAC means only CloudFront can read the bucket.

rejects.ec2: No server needed: S3 holds the files and CloudFront serves them.
rejects.beanstalk: Elastic Beanstalk runs app servers. Static files don't need one.
rejects.rds: A static site has no database. The files live in S3.
rejects.apigateway: API Gateway fronts APIs. CloudFront serves static files straight from S3.

puzzles.title: Members-Only API
puzzles.story: The city library app lets members sign in and save their reading lists. Only signed-in members may call the API, and each member must only see their own list.
requirements: Users sign up and sign in with email
The API rejects requests without a valid token
Business logic runs without servers
Reading lists are stored in a fast, serverless database
puzzles.why: Cognito user pools authenticate members and issue JWTs (sign-in tokens). A Cognito authorizer on the API Gateway REST API validates the token before Lambda runs. Lambda takes the user ID from the token's claims and uses it as the DynamoDB partition key, so each member only ever reads their own items.
puzzles.simpleWhy: Cognito checks who members are and hands them a pass. The gateway checks the pass, so each member only sees their own things.

operational.tip: Enable API Gateway access logs and Lambda metrics to trace every request.

security.tip: Validate tokens at the API and give Lambda a least-privilege role. DynamoDB encrypts at rest by default; use a customer managed KMS key when you need to control and audit the key.

reliability.tip: DynamoDB replicates across AZs; enable point-in-time recovery against accidental deletes.

performance.tip: Key by user ID for single-digit millisecond lookups; let API Gateway reject bad tokens so invalid calls never invoke Lambda.

cost.tip: On-demand DynamoDB, Lambda and API Gateway bill per request, and Cognito bills per monthly active user. With no servers, an idle app costs almost nothing.

sustainability.tip: Fully managed serverless services share infrastructure efficiently, so no dedicated servers sit idle.

puzzles.title: Market Day Orders
puzzles.story: On market day the bakery gets thousands of orders in minutes. The order API must never drop an order, even if the back office is slow or a bad order breaks processing.
requirements: Accept orders instantly through an API
Buffer orders so processing can catch up
Retry failures and isolate orders that keep failing
Store processed orders durably
puzzles.why: API Gateway writes each order to an SQS queue and returns immediately, so customers never wait on processing. Lambda polls the queue in batches and writes to DynamoDB. Messages that fail repeatedly move to a dead-letter queue instead of blocking the line. Standard queues deliver each message at least once, so make processing idempotent (safe to run twice).
puzzles.simpleWhy: Orders wait in a queue, so customers never wait. Lambda works through them, and broken ones are set aside instead of blocking the line.

operational.tip: Alarm when the dead-letter queue is not empty and when queue age grows.

security.tip: Encrypt the queue and let only the API role send and the worker role receive.

reliability.tip: Add a DLQ with maxReceiveCount of at least 5. Set the visibility timeout to at least six times the function timeout. Give the DLQ a longer retention period than the source queue, so failed orders aren't lost or retried forever.

performance.tip: Lambda scales pollers with queue depth; tune batch size and use partial batch responses.

cost.tip: Queues let a smaller consumer absorb peaks instead of provisioning for the busiest minute.

sustainability.tip: Buffering smooths demand so fewer resources run at higher utilisation.

puzzles.title: Lake of Receipts
puzzles.story: Years of city shop receipts sit as CSV files in S3. Analysts want to query them with SQL, but the finance team's salary columns must stay hidden from everyone else.
requirements: Keep raw data in low-cost storage
Discover the schema automatically
Query with SQL without running servers
Restrict access down to specific columns
puzzles.why: S3 holds the data, a Glue crawler works out the schemas and writes them to the Glue Data Catalog, and Athena queries the files in place with SQL. Lake Formation grants table and column permissions centrally, so analysts see receipts but not restricted columns, and Athena enforces those grants.
puzzles.simpleWhy: Receipts sit in S3, Glue labels them, Athena answers questions right where they are, and Lars decides who sees which columns.

operational.tip: Schedule crawlers and ETL jobs, and monitor their runs, instead of editing schemas by hand.

security.tip: Grant column-level permissions in Lake Formation and encrypt data and query results with KMS.

reliability.tip: S3 durability plus versioning protects the raw zone from accidental overwrites.

performance.tip: Convert CSV to partitioned Parquet with Glue or an Athena CTAS (CREATE TABLE AS SELECT) query so queries read less data.

cost.tip: Athena bills by data scanned. Partition, compress and use columnar formats to scan less, and set workgroup scan limits.

sustainability.tip: Query in place instead of copying data, and lifecycle old raw files to colder storage.

rejects.ec2: Glue and Athena are serverless. No EC2 needed.
rejects.ebs: EBS is a block disk for EC2 servers. The lake lives in S3.

puzzles.title: Ask the Staff Helper
puzzles.story: City Hall staff keep asking the people team the same policy questions. Build a signed-in assistant that answers from the official staff handbook, remembers each employee's context and can file leave requests.
requirements: Only employees can use the assistant
Answers come from the staff handbook, with citations
The agent remembers context across conversations
The agent can call an internal leave API as a tool
Answers avoid off-limits topics and personal data leaks
puzzles.why: Employees sign in with Cognito. AgentCore Identity validates their tokens, then the agent runs in an isolated AgentCore Runtime session. For grounded answers, it retrieves handbook passages from a Bedrock Knowledge Base built on documents in S3. AgentCore Memory keeps each employee's context. AgentCore Gateway exposes the leave API (for example, a Lambda target) as an MCP tool the agent can call. Bedrock Guardrails filter off-limits topics and sensitive data.
puzzles.simpleWhy: Staff sign in, then a safe agent looks up answers in the handbook, remembers each person, can use the leave tool and stays on topic.

operational.tip: Use AgentCore Observability traces in CloudWatch to see each reasoning step and tool call.

security.tip: Authenticate every user, scope the agent's tool permissions tightly, and apply Bedrock Guardrails.

reliability.tip: Managed runtime and model endpoints leave no servers of yours to fail. Handle throttling with retries and backoff.

performance.tip: Retrieve only relevant chunks and pick the smallest model that passes your quality evaluations.

cost.tip: Pay per token and per use; prompt caching and right-sized models cut spend.

sustainability.tip: RAG over existing documents avoids training or fine-tuning a custom model.

puzzles.title: Two-Continent Booking System
puzzles.story: The city's hotel booking service now has guests in Europe and North America. It must stay fast for both and keep working if an entire AWS Region has problems.
requirements: Low-latency reads for users on both continents
Data replicated to a second Region
Traffic moves to the healthy Region automatically
Recovery without manual database rebuilds
puzzles.why: DynamoDB global tables keep multi-active replicas in each Region, so apps read and write locally. By default they use eventual consistency (MREC), where the last write wins, so two Regions could book the same room at once. To prevent that, create the table with multi-Region strong consistency (MRSC), or send each hotel's bookings to one home Region. MRSC uses exactly three Regions: three replicas, or two replicas and a witness. Route 53 latency routing with health checks sends users to the lowest-latency healthy Region. Failover routing is the alternative: it sends users to a standby Region when the primary fails. For relational data, Aurora Global Database has one writer Region and low-lag read replicas in others. It offers a managed cross-Region failover that you start, and that typically completes within minutes. ElastiCache Global Datastore can add a cross-Region cache for faster reads. It is a cache, not the booking system of record, and you promote its Region manually.
puzzles.simpleWhy: Copies of the bookings live on both continents, so everyone books nearby. Careful rules stop two people booking the same room.

operational.tip: Monitor replication latency and rehearse Region failover regularly (game days).

security.tip: Encrypt replicas with keys in each Region and keep IAM policies consistent across Regions.

reliability.tip: Multi-Region data plus health-checked DNS failover removes the Region as a single point of failure. With MRSC, a Region failover loses no confirmed bookings.

performance.tip: Latency-based routing and local replicas keep response times low on every continent.

cost.tip: Replicate only the tables that truly need more than one Region. Replicated writes and data transfer cost extra.

sustainability.tip: Serverless, on-demand replicas scale with each Region's traffic, so no Region sits on idle provisioned capacity.

puzzles.title: Storm at the Gates
puzzles.story: The city ticket shop opens sales for the summer festival and expects both a huge rush and attackers trying to flood or scrape the site.
requirements: Absorb network-layer floods far from the origin
Block SQL injection and abusive request rates
Keep DNS up under attack
Let the origin accept traffic only from the edge
puzzles.why: Route 53 and CloudFront spread traffic across AWS's global edge, where Shield Standard mitigates common network and transport layer attacks automatically. AWS WAF on the distribution adds managed rules, including the Anti-DDoS rule group, and rate-based rules for application-layer abuse. The origin accepts only CloudFront traffic. Shield Advanced adds service credits for attack-driven cost spikes. With Business Support+, Enterprise Support or Unified Operations, it also gives access to the Shield Response Team.
puzzles.simpleWhy: Worldwide front gates soak up floods for free, guard rules catch the sneaky attacks, and the app only lets CloudFront in.

operational.tip: Put WAF blocked-request metrics on a dashboard and alarm on traffic spikes.

security.tip: Start with AWS Managed Rules plus a rate-based rule. Tune them in count mode before you switch them to block.

reliability.tip: Globally distributed DNS and edge capacity keep serving while attacks are absorbed.

performance.tip: Caching static pages at the edge keeps the origin free for real purchases.

cost.tip: Filtering at the edge stops attack traffic before it scales up your backend and your bill.

sustainability.tip: Dropping bad traffic early avoids wasted compute on requests that should never run.

edges.caption: Traffic lands at CloudFront edges. Shield absorbs floods and WAF blocks bad requests.

edges.caption: CloudFront adds a secret header, and a WAF rule on the REST API lets only those in.

rejects.guardduty: GuardDuty detects threats and reports findings. It doesn't absorb or block a flood.
rejects.elasticache: A cache behind the origin speeds up reads, but a flood still reaches it. Stop it at the edge.
rejects.kms: KMS manages encryption keys. It doesn't filter or absorb traffic.
rejects.redshift: Redshift runs analytics. It plays no part in surviving an attack.

puzzles.title: The Night Watch
puzzles.story: The security team wants every API call in the city recorded, threats detected automatically, and a compromised access key disabled within minutes, even at 3 a.m.
requirements: Record who did what, when, across the account
Detect suspicious behaviour continuously
Route findings to automated responders
Notify humans and keep an audit trail of the response
puzzles.why: CloudTrail records API activity, and a trail stores it in S3 for long retention. GuardDuty analyses CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs to raise findings. Findings flow to EventBridge, where rules match high-severity types and invoke a Lambda responder. The responder deactivates keys or isolates resources and notifies the team via SNS.
puzzles.simpleWhy: CloudTrail keeps the diary, GuardDuty spots trouble in it, and EventBridge wakes a Lambda that locks things down and tells the team.

operational.tip: Codify incident runbooks as automated responses and test them regularly.

security.tip: Use an organization trail with log file validation and encrypt logs with KMS.

reliability.tip: Give the responder a DLQ or on-failure destination so no finding is silently dropped.

performance.tip: Filter precisely with event patterns so responders only run for relevant findings.

cost.tip: Keep long-term trails in S3 with lifecycle rules rather than in expensive hot log storage.

sustainability.tip: Event-driven responders run only when something happens, not on constant polling.

puzzles.title: Harbour Container Shop
puzzles.story: The harbour shop runs a containerised web API with a PostgreSQL database. The team is tired of patching servers and wants the product catalogue to load faster under heavy traffic.
requirements: Run containers without managing servers
Expose the API securely to the internet
Move PostgreSQL to Aurora, with Multi-AZ high availability
Cache hot catalogue reads
puzzles.why: An ECS service runs the API as tasks on Fargate, so there are no servers to patch. API Gateway reaches the tasks privately through a VPC link to an internal load balancer in front of them. With an HTTP API, Cloud Map service discovery can replace the load balancer. Aurora PostgreSQL provides a managed Multi-AZ database. ElastiCache serves hot catalogue reads from memory using cache-aside, which takes load off Aurora. The backend runs inside a VPC: the tasks, Aurora and ElastiCache sit in private subnets across two AZs.
puzzles.simpleWhy: Containers run on Fargate with no servers to patch. A cache serves popular items fast, and everything stays in private rooms.

operational.tip: Use rolling deployments with the circuit breaker (or ECS blue/green for quick rollback) and Container Insights.

security.tip: Keep tasks and databases in private subnets, give each task its own role, and encrypt Aurora with KMS.

reliability.tip: Spread tasks across AZs and let Aurora fail over to a replica automatically.

performance.tip: Cache-aside with sensible TTLs serves hot reads from memory; cache static assets at the edge.

cost.tip: Right-size task vCPU and memory, use Fargate Spot for work that can handle interruptions, and let caching shrink the database.

sustainability.tip: Managed, right-sized capacity and Aurora Serverless v2 scaling avoid idle over-provisioning.

puzzles.title: When a Region Goes Dark
puzzles.story: In 2026 a whole AWS Region was damaged, and AWS said data kept only in that Region could not be brought back. The city's order app runs in one Region today. Make sure that if its Region goes dark, customers are sent somewhere safe and no orders are lost for good.
requirements: Copies of the data in a second Region before anything breaks
Customers sent to the second Region automatically
The app can run in the second Region
The order table can be rebuilt from the copies
puzzles.why: Multi-AZ protects you when one building fails; only copies in another Region protect you when a whole Region is lost. When AWS's Bahrain Region was damaged in 2026, AWS told customers to recover from backups kept in other Regions. Export or back up the table to S3 and replicate that bucket to a second Region (or copy backups there with AWS Backup). Keep the app as code so it can be deployed again in minutes. Route 53 failover routing with health checks then answers with the second Region when the first one stops responding.
puzzles.simpleWhy: Two zones save you when one building fails. Losing a whole Region needs backups in another Region, ready to switch to.

operational.tip: Practise the failover on a calm day (a game day), so the first time isn't the real disaster.

security.tip: Encrypt the backup copies with a key that also exists in the second Region, or you can't read them there.

reliability.tip: Copies in another Region plus health-checked failover remove the Region as a single point of failure.

performance.tip: Health checks every few seconds mean customers are moved within minutes, not hours.

cost.tip: Backup and restore is the cheapest recovery plan: you pay for stored copies, not for a second app running all the time.

sustainability.tip: Serverless code in the second Region uses no energy until it's needed.
